title: Copy and Move: Writing the Five Operations Once, So You Never Have To Again

questions.question: What does the compiler generated copy constructor do with a raw pointer member?
options: Copies the address, so both objects point at the same memory
Refuses to compile
Sets the pointer to null in the copy
Copies the memory the pointer refers to
questions.explanation: It copies each member, and a pointer member is an address. Two owners then both release it, which corrupts the heap and usually crashes somewhere unrelated.

questions.question: What is the rule of zero?
options: Never use raw pointers
Always write all five operations explicitly
Never allocate memory in a class
If every member manages itself, write none of the five operations and let the compiler generate them
questions.explanation: With members like vector, string and unique_ptr the generated versions are already correct, and correct for free. That is the shape most classes should have.

questions.question: Why is copy assignment harder than copy construction?
options: Because it returns a reference
Because it cannot allocate memory
The target already owns something, and the source might be the target itself
Because it runs after the destructor
questions.explanation: Releasing before reading breaks under self assignment. Copy and swap avoids both problems by building the copy before anything is modified.

questions.question: Why must a move constructor clear the source?
options: Because the compiler requires it
Because the source is no longer accessible
The source's destructor still runs, and it must not release what was taken
To make the move faster
questions.explanation: Taking the pointer is only half the job. Leaving the source holding the same address means two objects release it.

questions.question: What happens when a class declares a destructor and nothing else?
options: Nothing changes
The move operations are suppressed, so it silently falls back to copying
The copy operations are suppressed
The class becomes non copyable
questions.explanation: Declaring a destructor stops the compiler generating moves. It is a performance cliff with no diagnostic, and it is the usual reason a class that looks fine is slow.

questions.question: Why should move operations be marked noexcept?
options: It only affects compile time
Because the compiler requires it for move assignment
Because moves cannot throw anyway
std::vector only moves its elements while growing if their move promises not to throw, and copies them otherwise
questions.explanation: Vector must leave the old contents intact if reallocation fails, so without the promise it copies. The missing keyword is a silent, measurable slowdown.
